fixes.explanation: She isn't falling anywhere. She appears as a great sign in heaven, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head. The falling comes in verse 4, and that's stars being swept from the sky, not her. I'd be dizzy too if I had to keep track of who's dropping, so let's keep her right where the text puts her.

Yes, a huge red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven royal crowns on his heads. The woman is called a sign, and so is he, and that's a lot of sign for one sky. Both signs appear in heaven. You can tell this guy is trouble without any help from me.

The moon is under her feet, but verse 4 says what the dragon is ready for. He stood before the woman who was about to give birth, ready to devour her child as soon as she gave birth. The moon isn't part of that. The child is the one in danger, and that's a lot heavier than sky decorations.

It looks that way with the dragon standing right there, but the text says otherwise. Verse 5 says her child was caught up to God and to His throne. Verse 4 had the dragon ready to devour the child, but the text never says he reaches him. It tells us the child was caught up to God.
Right. The dragon is ready and waiting, but verse 5 says her child was caught up to God and to His throne. That's where the text takes the child. I'd love to have seen the look on all seven faces.

The text doesn't send her to a temple. It says the woman fled into the wilderness, where God had prepared a place for her. A wilderness is a different kind of place than a building. It's a place God prepared, and that's the part that matters.

Nebuchadnezzar was a real king of Babylon who came to Jerusalem and besieged it (Daniel 1:1). But he isn't who the dragon is. Verse 9 says the great dragon is that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan. This dragon isn't an earthly king, no matter how many crowns he's wearing.

The woman isn't part of this announcement. Verse 14 has her flying to her place in the wilderness, where she was nourished. The voice gives a different reason: the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down. That's the reason it names.

The text doesn't say he surrenders. It says he was hurled down, and then the voice says the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down. That's being thrown, not handing over crowns. I've never met a seven-headed fellow who surrenders politely.

Exactly. The voice says, “They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony.” The Lamb is Jesus, who is called “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). The voice names His blood and the word of their testimony.
The voice names something else. It says they conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony. Hands and courage aren't named there.
Yes, two wings of a great eagle. Verse 14 says she was given them to fly from the presence of the serpent to her place in the wilderness. Notice the verse says she was given the wings.

The text doesn't mention a cave. It says the woman was given two wings of a great eagle to fly from the presence of the serpent to her place in the wilderness. The wings carry her to that place. And the sea only comes up later, at the end of the chapter, where the dragon stands on the shore.

Michael is the archangel who disputed with the devil (Jude 1:9), and he fought the dragon in heaven in Revelation 12:7. But he isn't named in this scene. Verse 16 says the earth helped the woman and opened its mouth to swallow up the river. So the help comes from the earth, not from an angel's sword.

That's not what the text says. Verse 17 says the dragon was enraged at the woman and went to make war with the rest of her children. It doesn't send him back to heaven or to Michael. It has him standing on the shore of the sea.

Right. Verse 17 says the dragon was enraged at the woman and went to make war with the rest of her children, who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. The text has him going to make war with them, not going back to fight Michael. His anger takes him toward them.
